body_markdown:
Let’s say you’ve got a need—maybe even a need for speed. For six- and seven-figure price tags, any number of today’s exclusive supercars and hypercars will propel you in no time flat to triple-digit velocities. Now let’s say you’ve got a need for speed *and* a mortgage. Is it even possible to find triple-digit speeds on a budget? Why, yes it is!


We’re not talking a *mere* hundred miles an hour here, either, though certainly that’s fast enough to get you into trouble in most jurisdictions. No, if you’re after something more eye-watering, like, say 150 mph, then this list is for you. Because all of these cars, in #2 (excellent) condition, will not only get you there, but can do so for less than fifty-grand.


## 1991–99 Mitsubishi 3000GT VR4


Hagerty Marketplace/Roxy1977


**Average #2 Value:[$42,500–$49,600](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mitsubishi/3000_gt/1993/1993-mitsubishi-3000_gt-vr4?id=aCn1I000000CrHQSA0&condition=excellent)**


Often lost in the discussion that continues to buzz around the darlings of the early ’90s Japanese sports car invasion—the Z32 Nissan 300ZX, Toyota Supra Turbo, Mazda RX-7 FD, and Acura NSX—is the absolute boss-level techno-marvel that was the 3000GT VR4. Maybe that’s because it existed just outside the mainstream? Or because the 3000GT in other trims was also kind of a Dodge?


But what a successor to the Starion it was. In the realm of automotive party tricks, the VR4 seemingly had them all, especially the early cars of 1991–94. This included full-time all-wheel drive and four-wheel steering, electronically controlled suspension (ESC), active aerodynamics in the form of a front air dam and rear spoiler that changed position above 45 mph, a dual-mode exhaust, and pop-up headlights. A twin-turbocharged and intercooled V-6 initially made 300 horsepower and 307 lb-ft of torque, running through a five-speed gearbox. After ’94, output climbed to 320 hp and 315 lb-ft and a six-speed appeared, but by the end of production, the car had lost its unique exhaust, active aero, and ESC. In 1994, *[Car and Driver](https://www.caranddriver.com/reviews/a65488283/1994-mitsubishi-3000gt-vr4-archive-test/)* clocked a 3000GT VR4 from 0 to 60 mph in 5.1 seconds, with drag-limited top speed of 153 mph.


## 1999–2004 Porsche 911 Carrera & Carrera 4 Coupe


Hagerty Marketplace/EFP


**Average #2 Value:[$42,000–$45,000](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/2000/2000-porsche-911-carrera?id=aCn1I000000DFLJSA4)**


After decades of building 911 sports cars powered by air-cooled flat-six engines, Porsche did the unthinkable when it introduced the[996 generation](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/your-handy-porsche-996-buyers-guide/) : It added a radiator and liquid to flow through it. The change marked the biggest evolution in Porsche’s engineering philosophy since it had unveiled the front-engine 924 in 1976. And, if 911 values are anything to go by, people are still mad about it.


The change in cooling wasn’t the only gripe, of course, as fans bemoaned the 996’s softer lines and “fried egg” headlights. When the car’s infamous intermediate shaft (IMS) bearing issue surfaced, that became another cudgel with which to beat the car. But these lozenge-shaped Teutons are no joke on the road, and they were objectively better cars than their predecessors. Their 3.4-liter sixes initially delivered 296 hp and 258 lb-ft, enough to propel them to 60 mph in 4.9 seconds en route to a 174-mph top speed. The engine was stroked to 3.6 liters in 2002, which upped output to 320 horses and 273 lb-ft of torque and only sharpened its performance.


IMS issues have been addressed in many cars, though less can be done about the polarizing looks. You either love or hate (or simply tolerate) them. If you can do that, these 996s offer terrific value for exotic levels of performance, and prices for Carrera and all-wheel-drive[Carrera 4 models](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/911/2003/2003-porsche-911-carrera_4?id=aCn1I000000DPsFSAW&condition=excellent) tend to be quite similar across the entire generation


## 2001–04 Corvette C5 Z06


Hagerty Marketplace/BooneSCF


**Average #2 Value:[$33,100 for 2001](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2001/2001-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000Cu8OSAS&condition=excellent) ;[$38,700 for 2002–04](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/corvette/2003/2003-chevrolet-corvette-z06?id=aCn1I000000CrvHSAS&condition=excellent)**


Since Chevrolet first dropped a V-8 into its two-seater back in 1955, the Corvette has always represented great performance in an affordable package. Perhaps the pinnacle of that ethos is the fifth-generation[Z06](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/six-decade-corvette-z06-odyssey/) , so named as the nod to the high-performance package that debuted on the ’63 Split-Window.


In C5 Corvette guise, the Z06 hardtop package featured a track-focused suspension with stiffer springs and bigger sway bars, along with brake cooling ducts, fat tires, and some lightweight bits that shaved a few pounds from the standard Corvette of the day. Underhood for 2001 was the 385hp 5.7-liter LS6 V-8, which represented a 40-hp gain over a standard Vette. But Chevy went all-in just a year later, and the remainder of Z06s benefitted from a lighter valvetrain, revised cam, and a few other tweaks that brought output to 405 hp and an even 400 lb-ft, all running to the rear axle through a TREMEC T-56 six-speed. On the road (or the track, really), that equated to a 170-mph machine that could hit 60 mph in just 3.9 seconds.


To think that you can pick up an excellent, low-mileage example today for less than the cost of, well, just about anything, is nuts.


## 2003–10 Bentley Continental GT


Hagerty Marketplace


**Average #2 Value:[$28,000–$38,000](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/bentley/continental/2005/2005-bentley-continental-gt?id=aCn1I000000DHfISAW&condition=excellent)**


It’s difficult to overstate just how important the Continental GT was to the Bentley brand when it[debuted in 2003](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bentley-marks-20-years-of-the-continental-gt-with-a-one-off-and-a-world-tour/) . Five years after Volkswagen’s purchase of the storied British marque (and the infusion of cash that came with it), that first product *had* to be good. But it wasn’t good: It was stellar. After 80 years of upper-crust cottage manufacturing of limited-production, highly exclusive motor cars, here was a ballistic missile clad in a tuxedo and ready for the masses. That the $150,000 car’s arrival coincided with Bentley’s return not only to the 24 Hours of Le Mans but to the top step of the podium with the Speed 8’s overall victory was also a massive PR boost.


Power for the elegant all-wheel-drive grand tourer came from a 6.0-liter twin-turbocharged W-12 engine—about as far from the Z06’s naturally aspirated pushrod mill as it gets. Its 552-horsepower and 479 lb-ft of torque, available from just 1600 rpm, conspired to make the Conti the fastest Bentley ever built, with 60 mph coming in 4.7 seconds and 198 mph arriving if you stood on it long enough.


No doubt it is the most refined, most luxurious, most exotic, and fastest car on this list, but today’s low cost to get into an excellent one reflects the economic realities of keeping it that way: Although well-built, these are complicated cars and the costs associated with maintaining them properly can be substantial. You’ll sure look fabulous doing so, however, so there’s that.


## 2004–06 Pontiac GTO


Teddy Pieper – @vconceptsllc


Average #2 Value:[$24,600 for 2004](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/pontiac/gto/2004/2004-pontiac-gto-base?id=aCn1I000000DSqPSAW&condition=excellent) ;[$32,300 for 2005–06](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/pontiac/gto/2005/2005-pontiac-gto-base?id=aCn1I000000DWY3SAO&condition=excellent)


Twenty years ago, before Pontiac started circling the drain, GM’s excitement division went the captive import route to resurrect its most famous moniker. Based on Australia’s Holden Monaro, the new GTO arrived on these shores with a 5.7-liter LS1 V-8 underhood making 350 hp and 365 lb-ft. It was mated to either a four-speed auto or a TREMEC six-speed, and was capable of hitting 60 mph in 5.3 seconds, with a governed top speed of 158 mph.


The only problem, it seems, was the car’s snoozy looks. It wore Pontiac’s corporate nose, sure, but there was little exciting about its overall styling. As a result, it wasn’t quite the hot seller the division hoped it would be, which kind of makes it a super sleeper today. That’s doubly true for the 2005–06 models, which feature the 400-hp 6.0-liter LS2 but also dual hood scoops, which will surely alert Johnny Law to the car’s sporting pretentions.


Pontiac produced around 40,000 GTOs over three years, and today examples in excellent condition cost roughly what they did new. If modern-ish muscle is your thing, however, it’s worth seeking one out.


## Honorable Mention


- 1993–95 Dodge Viper RT/10 ($41,800 to $43,300)
- 2000–09 Honda S2000 ($43,600 for 2000–03 AP1; $49,900 for 2004–09 AP2)
- 2003–08 Mercedes-Benz SL55 AMG ($29,000)
- 2009–14 Cadillac CTS-V Sedan ($48,900)
- 2007–12 Ford Mustang Shelby GT500 Coupe ($44,100–$49,100)
